VIDEO.title: The Hidden Clue in Jesus’ HARDEST Rebuke!
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: If you have faith the size of a mustard seed…
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 17:14-27. Coming down from the mountain, Jesus finds a father whose son has seizures; the disciples could not cure him. Jesus calls them an unbelieving and perverse generation, rebukes the demon, and the boy is cured. Privately the disciples ask why they could not cast it out: 'Because of your little faith.' Faith the size of a mustard seed moves mountains. Jesus again foretells His death and resurrection. In Capernaum the collectors of the two-drachma tax question Peter, and Jesus provides a stater from a fish's mouth.

Mark gives the most detail (Mark 9:14-29): scribes arguing with the disciples, the father's 'I do believe; help my unbelief,' and 'This kind cannot come out by anything but prayer.' Some early manuscripts lack Matthew 17:21; the LSB prints it in brackets.

The disciples had been given authority over unclean spirits (10:1) and had cast out demons before. Luke says the meaning of the passion prediction was concealed from them (Luke 9:45). The tax collectors' question expects the answer yes.

'Unbelieving and perverse generation' recalls Deuteronomy 32, where Israel forgot the Rock who begot them. The video reads 'little faith' as misplaced faith, Peter's problem on the water (14:30-31): trusting their own efforts instead of Jesus' authority. They did not pray. The sons of Sceva show the same mistake (Acts 19:13-16).

The lesson: disciples of Jesus should never attempt the work of ministry by their own efforts and in their own strength; their success will come from the authority and ability that only Jesus can provide. The temple tax, paid by a fish, teaches the same.
QUOTES: Disciples of Jesus should never attempt to perform the work of ministry by their own efforts and in their own strength.
The phrase little faith is not describing the quantity of faith. It's describing a misplaced faith in the wrong thing.
Their success in ministry will come from the authority and the ability that only Jesus can provide.
They treat Jesus' authority as some kind of magic trick.

method.p: Much of what Jesus says alludes to earlier Scripture, connections the video calls remez, so that His disciples go back and wrestle with the deeper point. Here 'unbelieving and perverse generation' sends us to Deuteronomy 32.

LSB_QUOTES.text: And Jesus answered and said, “O you unbelieving and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I put up with you? Bring him here to Me.”

And He *said to them, “Because of your little faith; for truly I say to you, if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible to you.

However, so that we do not offend them, go to the sea and throw in a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; and when you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Take that and give it to them for Me and you.”

BOY.title: Lord, have mercy on my son

src.text: “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he has seizures and suffers terribly; for he often falls into the fire and often into the water. And I brought him to Your disciples, and they could not cure him.”

lines.text: Jesus leads Peter, James and John back down the mountain and finds the rest of the disciples trying and failing to cast out a demon.
Mark's account has the most detail: a large crowd, 'and scribes arguing with them' (Mark 9:14), and a dramatic convulsion as soon as the boy sees Jesus (Mark 9:20).

src.text: And Jesus said to him, “‘If You can?’ All things are possible to him who believes.” Immediately the boy’s father cried out and was saying, “I do believe; help my unbelief.”

lines.text: Before the exorcism Jesus talks with the father, which leads to teaching about faith and to the father's incredibly important words.

src.text: [But this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting.”]

lines.text: Some Bibles jump from verse 20 to verse 22, because some of the earliest manuscripts do not have this verse. The translators want to be careful.
The LSB keeps 17:21 in brackets. Mark's text reads, 'This kind cannot come out by anything but prayer' (Mark 9:29).

left.text: And while they were gathering together in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men; and they will kill Him, and He will be raised on the third day.” And they were deeply grieved.

right.text: But they did not understand this statement, and it was concealed from them so that they would not perceive it, and they were afraid to ask Him about this statement.

lines.text: Jesus tells them again so they will not be surprised, yet it seems He does not want them to understand yet. 'Who concealed it?' The video says that deserves its own meditation.

left.text: And summoning His twelve disciples, Jesus gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every kind of disease and every kind of sickness.

right.text: Now the seventy returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in Your name.”

lines.text: Jesus gave the disciples authority over unclean spirits, and they had moments of great victory over demons. Now they failed. Why?

left.text: And Jesus answered and said, “O you unbelieving and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I put up with you? Bring him here to Me.”

right.text: You neglected the Rock who begot you, / And forgot the God who brought you forth.

lines.text: In Deuteronomy 32 Israel dealt corruptly with God (32:5) and forgot the Rock who begot them; He calls them 'a perverse generation, / Sons in whom is no faithfulness' (Deuteronomy 32:20).
Why use these words of the disciples? Because they were not mindful of Jesus. They saw a problem, remembered they had authority, and tried to cast out the demon by their own efforts.

left.text: And immediately Jesus stretched out His hand and took hold of him, and *said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”

right.text: And He *said to them, “Because of your little faith; for truly I say to you, if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible to you.

lines.text: Peter started well on the water, then seemed to think he was keeping himself afloat; when his attention went to the wind, he sank. The disciples have Peter's problem.

So 'little faith' does not describe the quantity of faith in Jesus, the video says, but faith misplaced in the wrong thing. That is how Jesus can rebuke little faith and praise mustard-seed faith in one breath.

src.text: And the evil spirit answered and said to them, “I recognize Jesus, and I know about Paul, but who are you?” And the man, in whom was the evil spirit, leaped on them, subdued all of them, and utterly prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.

lines.text: Had the disciples prayed, they would have asked the Lord to act, aligning their efforts with His authority. Clearly they did not pray.

The sons of Sceva used Jesus' name without knowing Him, treating His authority as a magic trick. The lesson: never attempt the work of ministry in your own strength; success comes from the authority and ability only Jesus provides.

src.text: Now when they came to Capernaum, those who collected the two-drachma tax came to Peter and said, “Does your teacher not pay the two-drachma tax?” He *said, “Yes.” And when he came into the house, Jesus spoke to him first, saying, “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect tolls or taxes, from their sons or from strangers?”

lines.text: The Greek question expects a positive answer: 'Your teacher does pay the tax, does he not?'
Is Jesus saying Christians are exempt from all taxes? From temple taxes? Why a miracle for something as trivial as a tax? The video says Matthew placed this right after the demon for a reason.

TAX.title: Half a shekel for the sanctuary

src.text: This is what everyone who is numbered shall give: half a shekel according to the shekel of the sanctuary (the shekel is twenty gerahs), half a shekel as a contribution to Yahweh. Everyone who is numbered, from twenty years old and over, shall give the contribution to Yahweh.

lines.text: The tax goes back to Exodus 30:13 and 38:25-26: Israelite males twenty and over paid it for the sanctuary, later the temple.
The video cites Craig Blomberg that formal rabbis were exempt, so the question may have been about Jesus' legitimacy as a rabbi.

src.text: And when Peter said, “From strangers,” Jesus said to him, “Then the sons are exempt.

lines.text: Jesus answers with a parable-like picture: kings do not tax their own sons. As the Son of the King, He is free.
Peter has just confessed Him 'the Son of the living God' (16:16).

TAX.title: A stater in a fish's mouth

src.text: However, so that we do not offend them, go to the sea and throw in a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; and when you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Take that and give it to them for Me and you.”

lines.text: The same lesson as the boy: what the disciples need comes from Jesus' authority and ability, not their own resources.
A stater was a four-drachma coin, enough for two people's tax. Jesus pays 'so that we do not offend them.'

TERMS.def: The half-shekel paid yearly for the temple (Exodus 30:13). The captions write 'Draces' and 'drama.'
A silver coin worth four drachmas, enough for two. The captions write 'shekele.'
Greek oligopistia; the video reads it as faith placed in the wrong thing.
Casting out a demon. The captions write 'exercise.'
A hint back to Scripture. The captions write 'Rayim.'
A unit of text, such as one story. The captions write 'paricopies.'

WORDS.gloss: To have seizures; literally 'moonstruck.' Look up: BDAG, σεληνιάζομαι.
Little faith; related to oligopistos, 'you of little faith' (14:31).
Two-drachma coin, the half-shekel temple tax.
Rock, a name for God in Moses' song. Look up: BDB or HALOT, צור.

BACKGROUND.p: Exodus 30 sets a half-shekel 'contribution to Yahweh' for every man counted. In Jesus' day it was paid yearly in Tyrian coin, and money changers set up tables in Adar to collect it (Mishnah Shekalim 1:3). After AD 70 Rome redirected it to the temple of Jupiter.

The Mishnah exempts women, slaves and minors from pledges (Mishnah Shekalim 1:3) and records a debate about priests: one teacher said 'Any priest who contributes the half-shekel is not considered a sinner' (Mishnah Shekalim 1:4), while Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai disagreed. It does not mention rabbis.

Matthew's word means 'moonstruck,' an ancient name for seizures, and Matthew also says a demon came out (17:18). The Gospels keep illness and possession distinct in other places (4:24), so here they describe both.

WITNESSES.text: But by faith here He means that which related to the miracles, and mentions a mustard seed, to declare its unspeakable power.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 57, on 17:20. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: See how He neither declines the tribute, nor simply commands to pay it, but having first proved Himself not liable to it, then He gives it
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 58, on 17:27. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: I am indeed free from paying tribute. For if the kings of the earth take it not of their sons, but of their subjects; much more ought I to be freed from this demand
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 58, on 17:25-26. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

DEBATES.p: The video reads 'little faith' as faith misplaced in self. Others take it as weak or wavering faith in God, made strong not by size but by its object (the mustard seed).
The verse is missing from early manuscripts such as Sinaiticus and Vaticanus and may come from Mark 9:29. Many modern translations put it in a footnote; the LSB and NASB keep it in brackets.

DEBATES.h: What does the temple tax teach?
DEBATES.p: Readers see Jesus as the Son of the temple's King, freedom used to avoid needless offense, or (with the video) Jesus supplying what His disciples cannot.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: Luke 10:17 is the return of the seventy, not the Twelve; the video's point about earlier success still holds for the Twelve (Mark 6:13).
The claim from Craig Blomberg that formal rabbis were exempt from the tax is not sourced in the video. The Mishnah discusses priests (Mishnah Shekalim 1:4), not rabbis.
The video quotes 'faithless and twisted generation'; the LSB has 'unbelieving and perverse generation' (17:17).
Reading 'little faith' as misplaced faith is the video's interpretation; the teacher says, 'I could be wrong about that.'
In Mark it is the boy who falls to the ground when he sees Jesus (Mark 9:20).
The captions write 'Draces' and 'drama' for drachma, 'shekele' for stater, 'exercise' for exorcise, 'Rayim' for remez, 'Keva' for Sceva, and 'paricopies' for pericopes.

XREFS.label: John 15:5
XREFS.why: Apart from Me you can do nothing

QUESTIONS: The disciples had real authority and still failed. What changed?
'I do believe; help my unbelief.' When have you prayed something like that?
Is your faith small, or is it pointed at the wrong thing?
Where are you trying to do God's work in your own strength? What would prayer change?
Why do you think Jesus paid a tax He did not owe?
How does the fish with a coin teach the same lesson as the boy?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson, stated plainly: disciples of Jesus should never attempt to perform the work of ministry by their own efforts and in their own strength. Instead, they must recognize that their success in ministry will come from the authority and the ability that only Jesus can provide. That explains Jesus' frustration and His allusion to Deuteronomy 32: the disciples were not mindful of Him. Had they prayed, they would have asked the Lord to move on their behalf, aligning their efforts to His authority. The sons of Sceva made the same mistake, treating Jesus' authority as a magic trick, and were beaten and embarrassed. The teacher asks viewers to work out for themselves how the temple-tax story teaches the same lesson.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): before your next act of service, at home, church or work, stop and pray Mark 9:24 and John 15:5. Afterward, write one sentence about what Jesus did that you could not.

   (video) So 'little faith' does not describe the quantity of faith in Jesus, the video says, but faith misplaced in the wrong thing. That is how Jesus can rebuke little faith and praise mustard-seed faith in one breath.
4. Acts 19:13-16: The sons of Sceva
   Warning Acts 19:15-16: "And the evil spirit answered and said to them, “I recognize Jesus, and I know about Paul, but who are you?” And the man, in whom was the evil spirit, leaped on them, subdued all of them, and utterly prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Acts+19:15-16
   (video) Had the disciples prayed, they would have asked the Lord to act, aligning their efforts with His authority. Clearly they did not pray.
   (video) The sons of Sceva used Jesus' name without knowing Him, treating His authority as a magic trick. The lesson: never attempt the work of ministry in your own strength; success comes from the authority and ability only Jesus provides.

## The two-drachma tax
1. Matthew 17:24-25: Does your teacher not pay?
   Yes Matthew 17:24-25: "Now when they came to Capernaum, those who collected the two-drachma tax came to Peter and said, “Does your teacher not pay the two-drachma tax?” He *said, “Yes.” And when he came into the house, Jesus spoke to him first, saying, “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect tolls or taxes, from their sons or from strangers?”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+17:24-25
   (video) The Greek question expects a positive answer: 'Your teacher does pay the tax, does he not?'
   (video) Is Jesus saying Christians are exempt from all taxes? From temple taxes? Why a miracle for something as trivial as a tax? The video says Matthew placed this right after the demon for a reason.
2. Exodus 30:13-14: Half a shekel for the sanctuary
   Temple tax Exodus 30:13-14: "This is what everyone who is numbered shall give: half a shekel according to the shekel of the sanctuary (the shekel is twenty gerahs), half a shekel as a contribution to Yahweh. Everyone who is numbered, from twenty years old and over, shall give the contribution to Yahweh." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Exodus+30:13-14
   (video) The tax goes back to Exodus 30:13 and 38:25-26: Israelite males twenty and over paid it for the sanctuary, later the temple. (Exodus 38:25-26)
   (video) The video cites Craig Blomberg that formal rabbis were exempt, so the question may have been about Jesus' legitimacy as a rabbi.
3. Matthew 17:25-26: Then the sons are exempt
   Son Matthew 17:26: "And when Peter said, “From strangers,” Jesus said to him, “Then the sons are exempt." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+17:26
   (video) Jesus answers with a parable-like picture: kings do not tax their own sons. As the Son of the King, He is free.
   [Background] Peter has just confessed Him 'the Son of the living God' (16:16). (Matthew 16:16)
4. Matthew 17:27: A stater in a fish's mouth
   Provision Matthew 17:27: "However, so that we do not offend them, go to the sea and throw in a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; and when you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Take that and give it to them for Me and you.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+17:27
   (video) The same lesson as the boy: what the disciples need comes from Jesus' authority and ability, not their own resources.
   [Background] A stater was a four-drachma coin, enough for two people's tax. Jesus pays 'so that we do not offend them.'

## Key people
- The father: Kneels, begs mercy for his son, and cries 'help my unbelief' (Mark 9:24). [Background] Luke adds that the boy was his only son (Luke 9:38).
- The boy: Has seizures and falls into fire and water; cured at once. [Background] Mark says the spirit made him mute (Mark 9:17).
- The disciples: Could not cast it out; little faith, relying on themselves. [Background] They had been sent with authority (10:1).
- Peter: Answers 'Yes' about the tax; sent to catch the fish. [Background] His little faith on the water is the video's key to 17:20 (14:31).
- The tax collectors: Collect the two-drachma temple tax in Capernaum. [Background] Not the Roman toll collectors like Matthew, but collectors for the temple.
- The sons of Sceva: Used Jesus' name like magic and were overpowered. [Background] Sceva is called 'a Jewish chief priest' (Acts 19:14).

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum (named in the video): Where the temple tax collectors come to Peter (17:24), and where Peter's house was (8:14).
- Bethsaida: Peter's hometown (John 1:44).
- Magdala: A fishing town on the west shore.
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas' capital on the lake.

## Key terms
- Two-drachma tax: The half-shekel paid yearly for the temple (Exodus 30:13). The captions write 'Draces' and 'drama.'
- Stater: A silver coin worth four drachmas, enough for two. The captions write 'shekele.'
- Little faith: Greek oligopistia; the video reads it as faith placed in the wrong thing.
- Exorcism: Casting out a demon. The captions write 'exercise.'
- Remez: A hint back to Scripture. The captions write 'Rayim.'
- Pericope: A unit of text, such as one story. The captions write 'paricopies.'

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- The temple tax: Exodus 30 sets a half-shekel 'contribution to Yahweh' for every man counted. In Jesus' day it was paid yearly in Tyrian coin, and money changers set up tables in Adar to collect it (Mishnah Shekalim 1:3). After AD 70 Rome redirected it to the temple of Jupiter.
- Who was exempt?: The Mishnah exempts women, slaves and minors from pledges (Mishnah Shekalim 1:3) and records a debate about priests: one teacher said 'Any priest who contributes the half-shekel is not considered a sinner' (Mishnah Shekalim 1:4), while Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai disagreed. It does not mention rabbis.
- Seizures and demons: Matthew's word means 'moonstruck,' an ancient name for seizures, and Matthew also says a demon came out (17:18). The Gospels keep illness and possession distinct in other places (4:24), so here they describe both.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "But by faith here He means that which related to the miracles, and mentions a mustard seed, to declare its unspeakable power." Homilies on Matthew 57, on 17:20. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "See how He neither declines the tribute, nor simply commands to pay it, but having first proved Himself not liable to it, then He gives it" Homilies on Matthew 58, on 17:27. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "I am indeed free from paying tribute. For if the kings of the earth take it not of their sons, but of their subjects; much more ought I to be freed from this demand" Homilies on Matthew 58, on 17:25-26. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Little faith: amount or object? The video reads 'little faith' as faith misplaced in self. Others take it as weak or wavering faith in God, made strong not by size but by its object (the mustard seed).
- Matthew 17:21 The verse is missing from early manuscripts such as Sinaiticus and Vaticanus and may come from Mark 9:29. Many modern translations put it in a footnote; the LSB and NASB keep it in brackets.
- What does the temple tax teach? Readers see Jesus as the Son of the temple's King, freedom used to avoid needless offense, or (with the video) Jesus supplying what His disciples cannot.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- Luke 10:17 is the return of the seventy, not the Twelve; the video's point about earlier success still holds for the Twelve (Mark 6:13).
- The claim from Craig Blomberg that formal rabbis were exempt from the tax is not sourced in the video. The Mishnah discusses priests (Mishnah Shekalim 1:4), not rabbis.
- The video quotes 'faithless and twisted generation'; the LSB has 'unbelieving and perverse generation' (17:17).
- Reading 'little faith' as misplaced faith is the video's interpretation; the teacher says, 'I could be wrong about that.'
- In Mark it is the boy who falls to the ground when he sees Jesus (Mark 9:20).
- The captions write 'Draces' and 'drama' for drachma, 'shekele' for stater, 'exercise' for exorcise, 'Rayim' for remez, 'Keva' for Sceva, and 'paricopies' for pericopes.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. The disciples had real authority and still failed. What changed?
2. 'I do believe; help my unbelief.' When have you prayed something like that?
3. Is your faith small, or is it pointed at the wrong thing?
4. Where are you trying to do God's work in your own strength? What would prayer change?
5. Why do you think Jesus paid a tax He did not owe?
6. How does the fish with a coin teach the same lesson as the boy?

## Application
- (video) The lesson, stated plainly: disciples of Jesus should never attempt to perform the work of ministry by their own efforts and in their own strength. Instead, they must recognize that their success in ministry will come from the authority and the ability that only Jesus can provide. That explains Jesus' frustration and His allusion to Deuteronomy 32: the disciples were not mindful of Him. Had they prayed, they would have asked the Lord to move on their behalf, aligning their efforts to His authority. The sons of Sceva made the same mistake, treating Jesus' authority as a magic trick, and were beaten and embarrassed. The teacher asks viewers to work out for themselves how the temple-tax story teaches the same lesson.
- Study note (added): before your next act of service, at home, church or work, stop and pray Mark 9:24 and John 15:5. Afterward, write one sentence about what Jesus did that you could not.
